newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA PUBLISHES TRANSPORT POLICY PAPER.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA PUBLISHES TRANSPORT POLICY PAPER.

text.p: Transport Minister Mac Maharaj on Wednesday published a policy blueprint which, he said, would transform South Africa's transport industry.

"We should not underestimate the challenge of this white paper. It brings about a fundamental shift in transport policy," he told a news conference after the document had been approved by the cabinet.
Maharaj summarised the impact of the policy document as a shift from "top down" policy formulation to a "bottom up" process driven by consumer needs.
He said the government would retain its regulatory role, but would emphasise strategic planning and shift towards a tender system for basic transport provision in place of the current licence system.
This would mean that government would define the service needed in collaboration with users whereas, at present, operators defined the service and then sought a licence.

"The South African transportation system is inadequate to meet the basic accessibility needs -- to work, health care, schools, shops -- in many developing rural and urban areas," the white paper says.
"The needs of the community and customers will be determined and provided for by a transparent, consultative, coordinated and accountable process based on comprehensive information."
Policy statements and proposals cover a wide range of issues from rail passenger transport to road and freight issues.
Maharaj said it would be impossible to abolish passenger transport subsidies within less than 10 to 15 years, but said there would be no direct subsidisation of minibus taxis.
The white paper stresses the role of diesel as the fuel of commercial travel and says a reduction in the price could boost competitiveness and economic growth.

"The introduction of a significant differential between the price of diesel and petrol fuels in line with world practice will be considered in consultation with the Liquid Fuels Task Group and the departments of mineral and energy affairs and finance," it says.
The white paper adds that road building and maintenance, maritime survey and safety services and aviation safety services could better be provided by "professionally managed arms-length agencies."
Principle roads, railways, airports, harbours and pipelines should be paid for by direct charges, though roads could be funded partly by a dedicated fuel levy and partly by tolls.

"Selected ports and airports will be elevated to the status of hubs in keeping with international trends and properly equipped to maximise South Africa's participation in the global economy," the document says.
Where appropriate, the government would establish transport infrastructure as an incentive to privately funded development.
The white paper sets a 40 km or one-hour acceptability limit on commuter travel to and from work and calls for an 80:20 ratio between public transport and private car usage.
Minibus taxis will become an integral part of the planned transport network and eligible for tenders, but will be regulated and licenced.
"The number of (taxi) permissions granted on a route or network will be determined by need estimated in terms of the passenger transport plan," the document says.

Maharaj said taxi operators would, in turn, by offered assistance in the form of business and operator training and said taxi cooperatives could be offered up to 36 fuel-station licences around the country as an additional source of income.
The policy document says government will continue to promote deregulation of land freight transport within strict safety and quality parameters.
But it adds: "Government will strive to level the playing fields to enable fair competition between the various land transport modes."
